title: The seed with nothing inside
hookLine: a father has his son break a banyan seed until there's nothing to see, and the smallest verb carries the week
carry: tat tvam asi: the unseen essence is you
tomorrow: a blind king asks one question. which word gives him away?

cards: Uddalaka has one more lesson for his son. Bring me a fruit from that banyan tree, he says. Shvetaketu brings it.
Break it. What do you see? Tiny seeds, sir.
Break one. What do you see? Nothing at all, sir.
And the father says: that finest essence you can't see, from it this whole great banyan stands. That finest essence is the self of everything. That is the real.

teach.b: That, you are. Three words, and the one doing the heavy lifting is the smallest: asi, you are. It belongs to the smallest verb there is, to be.

teach.h: TAPAS · ATMAN · ONE OR TWO · SO 'HAM · GUEST · ONE FAMILY.
teach.b: Asmi, I am, from so 'ham asmi. Asi, you are, from tat tvam asi. Asti, is, hiding inside nasti, is not.
Same core, as, with mi for I, si for you, ti for he, she or it. Now run the week back through that seed: a king who burned off his anger in tapas and was called a seer.
A warrior told that the atman is never born and never dies. Two schools hearing tat tvam asi as one, or as forever two. A voice behind the sun saying so 'ham asmi.
A guest welcomed like God. The earth as one family, because one Self lives in all. Every one of those leans on to be.
That's why the next stretch of the path starts a list of two hundred core words, the plain ones these texts keep returning to, with asmi, asi and asti.

teach.h: THE SMALLEST WORDS HOLD THE BIGGEST CLAIMS.
teach.b: The biggest claim Hindu scripture makes about who you are rests on the smallest word.

And many teachers read it as something to live by: on the days you feel like only your grades, your job or your worst mistake, the Upanishad points underneath, to an essence nobody can see and nothing can break.
A seed you can't see holds up a tree.

how: Sanskrit learners usually start with the present forms of as, to be, and a short list of words that recur in the Gita and the Upanishads, reading verses with a word-by-word gloss.

games.q: the verb to be — tap the pairs.

s: in the Chandogya, Shvetaketu breaks the seed and finds nothing
that unseen essence, his father says, is what the great banyan stands on, and what you are.
na plus asti, the a's melted: is not.
tat tvam asi has no verb in it
asi, you are, is the verb.

games.q: your little cousin asks what tat tvam asi means, word by word. what do you say?
o: tat, that; tvam, you; asi, are: that unseen essence, you are it.
tat, you; tvam, are; asi, God: it means you are God.
it's one word for 'seed', from the father's story.
games.why: tat, that; tvam, you; asi, are. in the seed story, 'that' is the finest essence nobody can see, from which the banyan stands.

practice: Say the three forms out loud, slowly, one per breath: asmi, I am; asi, you are; asti, it is. Then, like Shvetaketu, look at something small near you: a seed, a leaf, your own open hand.
Let tat tvam asi sit with it, without explaining. Then let the words go, and rest in simply being here.

wordCard.voice: Two hundred core words: the plain words a reader meets again and again. First up, the verb to be: asmi, asi, asti. The smallest verb, holding up the biggest line.

orig.note: Sanskrit: I am, you are, is: the present of as, to be.

carryVoice: Here's the line: tat tvam asi, the unseen essence is you. A week well walked.
